newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chubais under attack before Yeltsin operation.
newsitem.headline: Chubais under attack before Yeltsin operation.

text.p: Russian politicians took aim at the president's chief-of-staff, an appointee to the influential Security Council and the president himself in a new round of infighting before Boris Yeltsin's heart operation.

Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov said Yeltsin was not in control of Russia. Doctors have cancelled all Yeltsin's planned meetings while they carry out a final series of tests and decide exactly when to operate.
"The president as he is now cannot guide the ship, which is sailing in stormy seas almost without fuel and with the officers fighting on the bridge," Zyuganov told a news conference.

The mudslinging has been intensifying since last month when Yeltsin said he needed an operation to improve blood supply to his heart. Doctors, including pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, will meet on Monday to set the date.

The main criticism centres on the role of chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, who joined Yeltsin's team in July and has long been despised by conservatives who say his privatisation campaign sold off state property for a song.
"A covert political coup has taken place in Russia since the presidential election (last July)," Pavel Voshchanov, Yeltsin's former press secretary, wrote in Komsomolskaya Pravda.

"All power is now concentrated in the hands of representatives of the clan headed by Anatoly Chubais. He already has the essential things to make the president and the prime minister reckon with his interests."

The communists also say Chubais was behind the appointment of businessman and banker Boris Berezovsky as deputy secretary of the Security Council, which groups leaders of the government, the military and the security services.

"A shadow government of top Russian businessmen is no longer satisfied with a role of prompter, suggesting to the main administrators who to appoint, to sack and what to pay," the communist newspaper Pravda said on Thursday.
"The bankers want more. They want to be sitting at the controls so they can steer the structures of power."
The main casualty of infighting this week has been a special council set up by Yeltsin to encourage the government, parliament and the presidential apparatus to work together.
Yeltsin had said his "permanent four" -- Chubais, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and the heads of both houses of parliament -- should cooperate during his absence.
But the communist head of the lower house, the State Duma, said on Wednesday he would not work with Chubais and Chernomyrdin has postponed the first meeting of the council until next week.
He said Yegor Stroyev, chairman of the upper house, the Federation Council, would not have been able to attend on Friday, the date originally planned.

"If you want the council to work effectively three officials should take part -- the premier, the heads of the parliamentary chambers and of course the president," Zyuganov said. "There should not be regents like Chubais."

Chernomyrdin's own main headache surrounds Russia's dismal performance in collecting taxes, which the International Monetary Fund used as a reason to delay recommending the payment of a tranche of a $10 billion three-year loan.
The premier is chairing an emergency commission set up to encourage firms to pay the taxes they owe.
The commission has the same initials in Russian -- ChK -- as the secret police set up after the 1917 Bolshevik revolution and many Russians expect it to take draconian measures against tax debtors.
"The country is in such a situation that it cannot get any worse," Interfax news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying about tax arrears. "The ChK is only touching the tip of the iceberg."
